content.comment_body: Hello, I have a straightforward project using a [product_name] 24V unit with relay outputs. The setup includes a latching relay activated by two physical push buttons wired to the inputs, controlling a single coil output. Everything works initially, but at times the outputs turn off unexpectedly, as if someone pressed the stop button, though no such action occurs. I’ve also tried a conventional start-stop latching circuit with the same outcome—the outputs shut off. Even when simplifying the program to just a couple of lines, the issue persists. Could this be caused by electrical noise in the control cabinet? There are three inverters in the system, all controlled by the PLC outputs, but otherwise it’s a simple arrangement. Any advice or insights are greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!

If electromagnetic interference is the cause, add on-delays of around 0.1 seconds between the button and the latch. You might also want to troubleshoot the issue using diagnostic tools. For example, connect counters to all relevant inputs and monitor their values—if any counter increases without a button being pressed, electromagnetic issues may be present. Regards, [user_name]

Make sure the switch doesn’t suffer from voltage leakage. Also, ensure the [product_name]'s power supply is capable of properly powering the switch with adequate current. Check that the power line connection at the [product_name]'s terminal is secure and provides good contact.
Every terminal connection should be properly secured and have solid contact.

Check if supply issues are causing the PLC to restart at irregular intervals due to voltage disturbances. Inspect the supply voltage and consider enabling remanence on the latch to see if that resolves the problem.

Thank you all for your assistance. The issue was traced to an input drop from my 3SK2, which was just enough for the PLC to register, possibly related to the dark test feature of the 3SK2. Adding a counter as suggested resolved the problem. Much appreciated!

The thread explores possible causes such as input fluctuations from external devices and environmental issues like electromagnetic interference and unstable power supply. Troubleshooting strategies, including deploying counters for input diagnostics, proved effective in tracking and resolving the root cause of the problem.
